In [[mathematical analysis]], Haar's [[Tauberian theorem]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Haar|first=Alfred|date=December 1927|title=Über asymptotische Entwicklungen von Funktionen|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01209154|journal=Mathematische Annalen|language=de|volume=96|issue=1|pages=69–107|doi=10.1007/BF01209154|s2cid=115615866 |issn=0025-5831|url-access=subscription}}</ref> named after [[Alfréd Haar]], relates the asymptotic behaviour of a [[continuous function]] to properties of its [[Laplace transform]].  It is related to the [[integral]] formulation of the [[Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem]].

== Simplified version by Feller ==
[[William Feller]] gives the following simplified form for this theorem:<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Feller|first=Willy|date=September 1941|title=On the Integral Equation of Renewal Theory|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aoms/1177731708|journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics|language=en|volume=12|issue=3|pages=243–267|doi=10.1214/aoms/1177731708|issn=0003-4851|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Suppose that <math>f(t)</math> is a non-negative and continuous function for <math>t \geq 0</math>, having finite Laplace transform
:<math>F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t)\,dt</math>
for <math>s>0</math>. Then <math> F(s)</math> is well defined for any [[complex number|complex]] value of <math>s=x+iy</math> with <math>x>0</math>.  Suppose that <math>F</math> verifies the following conditions:

1. For <math>y \neq 0</math> the function <math>F(x+iy)</math> (which is [[holomorphic function|regular]] on the [[right half-plane]] <math>x>0</math>) has continuous boundary values <math>F(iy)</math> as <math>x \to +0</math>, for <math>x \geq 0</math> and <math>y \neq 0</math>, furthermore for <math>s=iy</math> it may be written as
: <math>F(s) = \frac{C}{s} + \psi(s),</math>
where <math>\psi(iy)</math> has finite [[derivative]]s <math>\psi'(iy),\ldots,\psi^{(r)}(iy)</math> and <math>\psi^{(r)}(iy)</math> is bounded in every finite [[interval (mathematics)|interval]];

2. The integral
:<math>\int_0^\infty e^{ity} F(x+iy) \, dy</math>
[[Uniform convergence|converges uniformly]] with respect to <math>t \geq T</math> for fixed <math>x>0</math> and <math>T>0</math>;

3. <math>F(x+iy) \to 0</math> as <math>y \to \pm\infty</math>, uniformly with respect to <math>x \geq 0</math>;

4. <math>F'(iy),\ldots,F^{(r)}(iy)</math> tend to zero as <math>y \to \pm\infty</math>;

5. The integrals
:<math>\int_{-\infty}^{y_1} e^{ity} F^{(r)}(iy) \, dy</math>    and     <math>\int_{y_2}^\infty e^{ity} F^{(r)}(iy) \, dy</math>
converge uniformly with respect to <math>t \geq T</math> for fixed <math>y_1 < 0</math>, <math>y_2 > 0</math> and <math>T>0</math>.

Under these conditions
:<math>\lim_{t \to \infty} t^r[f(t)-C] = 0.</math>

== Complete version ==
A more detailed version is given in.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lipka|first=Stephan|date=1927|title=Über asymptotische Entwicklungen der Mittag-Lefflerschen Funktion E_alpha(x)|url=http://acta.bibl.u-szeged.hu/13343/1/math_003_211-223.pdf|journal=Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged)|volume=3:4-4|pages=211–223}}</ref>

Suppose that <math>f(t)</math> is a continuous function for <math>t \geq 0</math>, having [[Laplace transform]]
:<math>F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t)\,dt</math>
with the following properties

1. For all values <math>s=x+iy</math> with <math>x>a</math> the function <math>F(s)=F(x+iy)</math> is [[holomorphic function|regular]];

2. For all <math>x>a</math>, the function <math>F(x+iy)</math>, considered as a function of the variable <math>y</math>, ''has the Fourier property'' ("Fourierschen Charakter besitzt") defined by Haar as for any <math>\delta>0</math> there is a value <math>\omega</math> such that for all <math>t \geq T</math>
:<math>\Big| \, \int_\alpha^\beta e^{iyt} F(x+iy) \, dy \; \Big| < \delta</math>
whenever <math>\alpha,\beta \geq \omega</math> or <math>\alpha,\beta \leq -\omega</math>.

3. The function <math>F(s)</math> has a boundary value for <math>\Re s = a</math> of the form
:<math>F(s) = \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{c_j}{(s-s_j)^{\rho_j}} + \psi(s)</math>
where <math>s_j = a + i y_j</math> and <math>\psi(a+iy)</math> is an <math>n</math> times [[differentiable]] function of <math>y</math> and such that the derivative
:<math>\left| \frac{d^n \psi(a+iy)}{dy^n} \right|</math>
is bounded on any finite interval (for the variable <math>y</math>)

4. The derivatives
:<math>\frac{d^k F(a+iy)}{dy^k}</math>
for <math>k=0,\ldots,n-1</math> have zero limit for <math>y \to \pm\infty</math> and for <math>k=n</math> has the Fourier property as defined above.

5. For sufficiently large <math>t</math> the following hold
:<math>\lim_{y \to \pm\infty} \int_{a+iy}^{x+iy} e^{st} F(s) \, ds = 0</math>

Under the above hypotheses we have the asymptotic formula
:<math>\lim_{t \to \infty} t^n e^{-at} \Big[ f(t) - \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{c_j}{\Gamma(\rho_j)} e^{s_j t} t^{\rho_j - 1} \Big] = 0.</math>
